propositions.text: Applicant is a Chinese citizen who applied for permanent residence in Canada as self-employed in May 2015, assisted by a licensed consultant.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Ms. Yintao Wu, is a citizen of the People’s Republic of China. In May 2015, she submitted an application for permanent residence in Canada as a member of the self-employed person’s class. The Applicant was assisted by a licensed immigration consultant [Consultant] based in Quebec, Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Chinese citizen who applied for Canadian permanent residence as self-employed in May 2015 with a licensed consultant's help.

propositions.text: On July 25, 2017, an officer emailed the applicant and spouse requesting an interview on August 21, 2017.
propositions.quote: On July 25, 2017, an Immigration Officer at the Consulate General of Canada in Hong Kong [Officer] sent a letter requesting that the Applicant and her spouse attend an interview on August 21, 2017.

propositions.text: The interview request was sent to the email address provided by the applicant in her representative form and application.
propositions.quote: The letter was sent to the e-mail address provided by the Applicant in her “Use of a Representative” form and her application for permanent residence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer emailed the applicant on July 25, 2017, requesting an interview, sent to the email address provided by the applicant.

propositions.text: On August 29, 2017, the officer rejected the application due to failure to attend the interview, assessing on available materials.
propositions.quote: On August 29, 2017, the Officer rejected the application for permanent residence. The Officer indicated that as the Applicant had failed to attend the scheduled interview, her application was assessed on the basis of the material available on file.

propositions.text: The officer decided the applicant did not qualify for permanent residence in the self-employed class.
propositions.quote: The Officer determined that the Applicant did not qualify for a permanent resident visa in the self-employed person’s class.

propositions.text: The decision was communicated to the applicant's consultant using the same email address as the interview request.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s decision was communicated to the Applicant’s Consultant using the same e-mail address as the one used to request the interview.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the officer rejected the application on August 29, 2017, for failure to attend interview and notified the consultant by the same email.

propositions.text: On September 4, 2017, the consultant emailed the visa office saying the interview request was never received and asked to reopen the file.
propositions.quote: On September 4, 2017, the Applicant’s Consultant sent an e-mail to the visa office in Hong Kong advising that the letter requesting an interview was never received. He also requested that the Applicant’s file be reopened so that she could be granted another opportunity to attend an interview.

propositions.text: Two days later, the visa office acknowledged the reconsideration request and said they would contact if the file was reopened.
propositions.quote: Two (2) days later, the visa office in Hong Kong acknowledged receipt of the Applicant’s request for reconsideration and indicated that if the delegated official decided to reopen the file, the Applicant and her Consultant would be contacted with information on the next steps.

propositions.text: The applicant and consultant received no further communication from the visa office.
propositions.quote: The Applicant and her Consultant have not received any further communication from the visa office.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the consultant requested reconsideration on September 4, 2017, claiming no interview request received; no further communication followed.

propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of the refusal decision dated August 29, 2017.
propositions.quote: The Applicant now seeks judicial review of the decision dated August 29, 2017 refusing her application for permanent residence as a member of the self-employed person’s class.

propositions.text: Applicant contends it was procedurally unfair to reject her application as she never received the interview request email.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that it was procedurally unfair to reject her application as she never received the July 25, 2017 e-mail requesting her to attend the interview.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the refusal was procedurally unfair because she never received the interview request email and seeks judicial review.

propositions.text: The key issue is who must bear the consequence of the failed communication: applicant or respondent.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this case is whether the Applicant or the Respondent must bear the consequence of the purportedly failed communication.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as who bears the consequence of the failed communication, applicant or respondent.

propositions.text: Respondent must prove on balance of probabilities that communication was correctly sent to applicant.
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence concerning failed communications requires that the Respondent first establish on a balance of probabilities that the communication (e-mail or otherwise) was correctly sent to the Applicant.

propositions.text: Once proven sent, there is a presumption the applicant received the communication.
propositions.quote: Once that is established, there is a presumption that the communication was received by the Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant may rebut presumption by credible evidence that communication was not received.
propositions.quote: However, the Applicant may rebut this presumption by demonstrating with credible evidence that the communication was not received (Fakeh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 547 at para 10; Chandrakantbhai Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 900 at paras 33, 40, 42 [Chandrakantbhai Patel]; Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 856 at para 16; Ghaloghlyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1252 at para 8 [Ghaloghlyan]; Zare v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1024 at para 37; Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 75 at para 14; Kaur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 935 at para 12; Yang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 124 at para 14).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the law: respondent must prove communication was sent; then presumed received; applicant may rebut with credible evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent has established on balance of probabilities that the interview request email was properly sent to the applicant.
propositions.quote: Upon review of the file, I am satisfied that the Respondent has established on a balance of probabilities that the e-mail requesting an interview was properly sent to the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent proved on balance of probabilities that the interview request email was properly sent to the applicant.

propositions.text: The certified record contains the email sent on July 25, 2017 to the consultant's email address provided by the applicant.
propositions.quote: A copy of the e-mail communication is contained in the Certified Tribunal Record [CTR] at page 16, and the request for an interview is included in the e-mail itself. The e-mail clearly demonstrates that it was sent on July 25, 2017 to the Consultant’s e-mail address, which had been provided by the Applicant in her application for permanent residence and on her “Use of a Representative” form.

propositions.text: The representative form authorizes Citizenship and Immigration Canada to send information to the provided email address.
propositions.quote: The latter form explicitly authorizes Citizenship and Immigration Canada to transmit information to the e-mail address provided.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the certified record contains the July 25, 2017 email sent to the consultant's authorized email address.

propositions.text: GCMS notes show the interview letter was sent on July 25, 2017 to the email declared on the representative form.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes pertaining to the Applicant’s file indicate that the interview convocation letter was sent to the Applicant on July 25, 2017. They also contain an entry from an officer who reviewed the file on August 25, 2017, confirming that the e-mail address in the GCMS was the same as the address declared on the “Use of a Representative” form.

propositions.text: An officer's GCMS entry on September 14, 2017 confirms the email was sent with no bounce-back or undeliverable message.
propositions.quote: Lastly, there is yet another GCMS entry, made by the Officer reviewing the Applicant’s reconsideration request on September 14, 2017, who writes that: Our email systems show that an email was sent on 25July2017(sic) at 1:05 pm, local time to [Consultant’s e-mail] advising of the interview. There was no bounce-back or undeliverable message.

propositions.text: The officer concluded the applicant was notified at valid contact info and failed to appear; no reply required.
propositions.quote: Based on my review, there is no error in fact or law. The applicant was notified of interview at the valid contact information on file and failed to appear. No reply required as standard no recon reply already sent.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes GCMS notes confirm the email was sent to the correct address with no bounce-back, and the applicant was notified but failed to appear.

propositions.text: Although an affidavit from the sending officer would be useful, its absence is not determinative.
propositions.quote: While it would have been useful for the Respondent to file an affidavit from the Officer who sent the e-mail communication on July 25, 2017, and to include a printout of his computer’s sent box as suggested by Justice Douglas R. Campbell in Ghaloghlyan, the failure to do so is not determinative.

propositions.text: Other evidence types may suffice to prove a communication was sent (Ghaloghlyan at para 10).
propositions.quote: In the same decision, Justice Campbell recognized that other types of evidence might suffice in proving that a communication was sent (Ghaloghlyan at para 10).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that although an affidavit from the sending officer would help, other evidence can suffice to prove the email was sent.

propositions.text: Respondent filed a paralegal affidavit attaching GCMS notes confirming the email was sent with no bounce-back.
propositions.quote: In the present case, the Respondent filed an affidavit from a paralegal in the Department of Justice attaching a copy of the GCMS notes pertaining to the Applicant. The GCMS notes are also contained in the CTR. In addition to the initial entry indicating that the e-mail was sent, two (2) other officers confirm that the e-mail communication was properly sent and that there was no bounce back or message indicating that it was undeliverable.

propositions.text: The GCMS notes' accuracy is unchallenged and the email copy is in the record; respondent met burden on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The accuracy of these notations in the GCMS notes has not been challenged and a copy of the e-mail communication is in the CTR. On the basis of the record before me and in the circumstances of this case, I am satisfied that the Respondent has met its burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the e-mail communication was correctly sent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent met its burden with unchallenged GCMS notes and affidavit confirming the email was sent properly.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to rebut presumption of receipt; mere statement of non-receipt is insufficient.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, on the other hand, has failed to rebut the presumption that the e-mail communication was received. I have considered the Applicant’s statement that she did not receive the e-mail requesting her attendance. However, it is insufficient to merely state that the e-mail in question was not received (Chandrakantbhai Patel at para 33).

propositions.text: Applicant did not provide evidence that the email address was unreliable, inactive, or malfunctioning.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not adduce any evidence, including from her Consultant, that the e-mail address was unreliable, inactive or malfunctioning.

propositions.text: Nothing on record suggests the email was not received by the consultant.
propositions.quote: In other words, there is nothing on the record that would leave me to believe that the e-mail communication was not received by her Consultant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant failed to rebut receipt presumption and gave no evidence the email address was unreliable or malfunctioning.

propositions.text: This case is distinguishable from Chandrakantbhai Patel where no copy of the alleged email was provided.
propositions.quote: In my view, the facts of this case are distinguishable from those in Chandrakantbhai Patel where the Respondent had failed to provide, and the CTR did not include, a copy of the alleged e-mail or a copy of the request letter bearing the same date (Chandrakantbhai Patel at paras 15, 42). That is not the case here.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case differs from Chandrakantbhai Patel because here a copy of the email was provided.

propositions.text: This case differs from Abboud and Asoyan where bounce-backs or inquiries indicated failed communication.
propositions.quote: They are also different from those found in Abboud v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 876 [Abboud] and in Asoyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 206 [Asoyan], upon which the Applicant relies in her written memorandum. In Abboud, the Court found that the automated replies received “after the e-mail had been sent should have raised doubts in the officer’s mind that the communication had failed” (Abboud at para 15). Similarly in Asoyan, the Court found that the applicant’s inquiry for an acknowledgment that her application had been received by the Sydney Centralized Intake Office on March 4, 2013 should have been an indication to the visa officer that she had not received the earlier e-mail requesting that she provide updated forms within a specified period of time (Asoyan at para 18). There is no such indication in the case at hand.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case differs from Abboud and Asoyan where bounce-backs or inquiries indicated failed communication, which is absent here.

propositions.text: Respondent proved email was sent to correct address and presumption of receipt not rebutted; applicant bears failed communication burden.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, as the Respondent has demonstrated on a balance of probabilities that the e-mail communication was sent to the correct e-mail address provided by the Applicant and the presumption of receipt has not been rebutted, the Applicant must bear the burden of the failed communication.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the respondent proved the email was sent and receipt presumed; applicant bears the failed communication burden.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is dismissed; no questions of general importance certified.
propositions.quote: For all of these reasons, the application for judicial review is dismissed. No questions were proposed for certification and I agree that none arise. JUDGMENT in IMM-4552-17 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is dismissed; No question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application and certifies no questions of general importance.
